title: A Very Simple Example of the Incompetence of Reporting on Marijuana Prohibition

content_html_sanitized:
Day before yesterday, I wrote about an editorial column in the New York Post, The Best Two Word Explanation for Marijuana Prohibition at The New York Post Is Amanda Devine, but, as noted that was an opinion column. It was just an exceptional example of outright duplicity, even for the Post.

 

However, as President Trump has suggested that he is thinking about discussing considering perhaps revisiting and/or reviewing the possibility of somehow changing the regulatory status of marijuana, being listed in Schedule One, the reporting on it has been demonstrably incompetent. Bad journalism made simple.

 

First, the simple facts. So how and why did marijuana get in Schedule One.

 

In 1971, President Nixon’s Attorney General, John Mitchell, who actually went to prison for his role in the Watergate scandal, put marijuana in Schedule One. This was not done one the basis of any scientific study. On the contrary. At about this time, Nixon also created a commission to study marijuana, The Schafer Commission.

 

From the Wikipedia article: “While the Controlled Substances Act was being drafted in a House committee in 1970, Assistant Secretary of Health Roger O. Egeberg had recommended that marijuana temporarily be placed in Schedule I, the most restrictive category of drugs, pending the Commission's report.

 

On March 22, 1972, the Commission's chairman, Raymond P. Shafer, presented a report to Congress and the public entitled "Marihuana: a Signal of Misunderstanding," which favored ending marijuana prohibition and adopting other methods to discourage use.”

 

Of course, Nixon rejected the recommendation of his own commission and simply left marijuana where it was supposed to be only temporarily. Now, over fifty years later it is still there and its status is being treated as though it was one of the Ten Commandments.

 

What really makes Schedule One different?

From the DEA: “Schedule I drugs, substances, or chemicals are defined as drugs with no currently accepted medical use and a high potential for abuse.”

 

So marijuana, which is legal for medical use in 40 states, is not recognized by the Federal Government as having any “currently accepted medical use.”

 

Other drugs included in Schedule One include heroin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD), 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (ecstasy), methaqualone, and peyote. Note that these drugs are not all alleged to be especially dangerous. Certainly peyote isn’t, but that they supposedly have “no  currently accepted medical use.”

 

Now consider some of the drugs that are in Schedule Two: including “cocaine, methamphetamine, methadone, hydromorphone (Dilaudid), meperidine (Demerol), oxycodone (OxyContin), fentanyl, Dexedrine, Adderall, and Ritalin.”

See

Marijuana Is In Schedule One. Fentanyl Is In Schedule 2. Think About It.

But fentanyl and these others are recognized as having “currently accepted medical use.” Actually, the scheduling process doesn’t seem to make much sense. Does anyone really believe that marijuana is comparable to fentanyl?

 

But the only legal difference between the two Schedules is whether it can be prescribed. But why does the scheduling process have any credibility?

See

Bush’s New Freedom Initiative: Treatment For Using Cannabis, From The Wonderful Folks Who Brought Us Vioxx, Baycol, Etc. Author of IOM Report Says, " I can't understand why it isn't rescheduled. "

 

But how is it being reported? That Trump is considering reclassifying marijuana as a “less dangerous drug.”

 

Less dangerous than what?
